passage: Karthik, sit down, the kolam can wait a minute. The Pongal I was fifteen, we had just moved to Madurai, and before I had met a single girl on our street I had decided they thought me a village oddity. So at the Pongal gathering on the Raghavans' terrace I stood by the water tank, arms folded, staring at the sky as if the whole thing bored me. Nobody came over. Of course nobody did; I looked like someone who wanted to be left alone. I went home and told my amma, 'See? They don't like me.' The next Pongal my cousin dragged me to the kolam contest and pushed a bowl of rice flour into my hands. A girl called Selvi laughed at my crooked lines, then showed me her own. That is how your Madhuri Atthai made her first friend on that street. The girls hadn't changed in a year. My face had.

qa.q: Where did Madhuri stand during the first Pongal gathering?
qa.a: She stood by the water tank on the terrace, arms folded, staring at the sky.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling as she stood apart looking bored?
qa.a: She felt anxious and already rejected, sure the girls thought her a village oddity, so she hid that fear behind a bored face.

qa.q: What turning point in the story broke Madhuri's pattern, and why did it work?
qa.a: Her cousin pushing her into the kolam contest put her among the girls with something to do, so Selvi could approach her and her old belief met new evidence.

qa.q: How might the girls on the street have seen Madhuri that first Pongal?
qa.a: They probably saw a newcomer who looked bored and wanted to be left alone, so leaving her be seemed polite rather than unkind.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose expectation of being disliked makes her act aloof and bored at a gathering, so others keep away and seem to prove her right.

passage:
Subject: Handover notes on the two juniors

Dear Prof. Iyer,

You asked for honest handover notes on the robotics club juniors.

In August I gave Naveen the gearbox redesign because he spoke confidently at the first meeting. I gave Pooja the parts inventory because she was quiet. I checked Naveen's drawings every evening, argued with him, sent him papers to read. Pooja's spreadsheets I glanced at once a week.

By November Naveen was explaining gear ratios to the second-years. Pooja was still counting screws, and she had stopped coming to the Friday build sessions.

Last week, short of hands, I asked her to debug the arm's sensor code. She found the fault in two days and asked me three sharp questions I couldn't answer.

I don't think the gap between them was ever talent. It was how much of my attention each one got. Please pass this to the next lead before they hand out tasks.

Ritu

qa.q: Which task did Ritu give Pooja in August?
qa.a: Ritu gave Pooja the parts inventory.

qa.q: What does Ritu seem to feel, looking back at the months of glancing at Pooja's spreadsheets once a week?
qa.a: Ritu seems uncomfortable and somewhat guilty, seeing that the gap between the juniors came from attention, not talent.

qa.q: What could the next club lead do differently with new juniors?
qa.a: Give every junior a stretching task early and the same regular feedback, instead of deciding from one meeting who is capable.

qa.q: What was it like for Pooja during the months of inventory work?
qa.a: Pooja got little feedback and no real challenge, so she probably felt overlooked, and she drifted away from the Friday sessions until a real problem showed what she could do.

grounding: Shows a mentor noticing that the junior trusted with challenging work and close attention grew, while the one given only simple tasks stalled.

subtype: Predicting failure and drifting into it [Actor]
passage: The Dasara dolls were already arranged on the wooden steps in the front room when Vidya's interview letter came from the government school in Hassan. 'They'll take someone from the city,' she told her brother Darshan, and slid the letter under the calendar. For the nine days of the festival she strung marigolds, handed out sundal to the neighbours' children, and opened her teaching notes only once, on the last night, turning pages without reading them. On the early bus to Hassan her hands were cold. When the panel asked how she would teach fractions to a class that was struggling, something she had done for the neighbours' children all summer, her mind went blank. She mumbled, apologised twice, and left before they finished. At home she dropped onto the mat and told Darshan, 'See? I knew it.' Darshan picked up the notes, still crisp and unmarked, and said nothing for a long moment.

qa.q: What did Vidya do with the interview letter when it arrived?
qa.a: She slid the letter under the calendar.

qa.q: Why did Vidya's mind go blank when the panel asked about fractions?
qa.a: She walked in frightened and certain she would fail, and that anxiety blocked something she knew well from teaching the neighbours' children all summer.

qa.q: What small step during the festival could have given Vidya a fairer chance?
qa.a: She could have set aside a short time on each of the nine days to read her notes and practise answers aloud, perhaps with Darshan asking the questions.

qa.q: How might Darshan see the result differently from Vidya?
qa.a: Darshan can see the crisp, unmarked notes, so to him the interview looks less like proof she was never good enough and more like the result of barely preparing.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose certainty that an interview will go badly leads to little preparation and a nervous performance, which she then takes as proof.

passage: I'm Vandana, and I've shared a desk with Ayesha at the architecture office for two years. She used to call the Friday client reviews 'the firing squad' and sit at the back, saying nothing. Last month that changed. Before the review for the new library project, she stayed late two evenings, pinning up printouts and practising out loud in the empty meeting room; I could hear her from the pantry. On Friday she spoke first, before the partner had even opened the file. Her voice shook for one sentence, then steadied. The client objected to the stairwell. She wrote it down, and on Monday she showed me her notebook: 'One objection, not ten.' I can't say what goes on in her head. But when our intern Raghav handed her a sloppy section drawing that afternoon, she didn't sigh at him the way she used to. She marked three fixes and said, 'You can get this right by Wednesday.' He did.

qa.q: What did Ayesha write in her notebook after the review?
qa.a: She wrote 'One objection, not ten.'

qa.q: What might Ayesha's shaky first sentence suggest about how she felt when she spoke first?
qa.a: She was probably still nervous and half expecting the old 'firing squad', but she spoke anyway, and her voice steadying hints at growing confidence.

qa.q: Which of Ayesha's choices helped most to break her old pattern, and why?
qa.a: Practising over two evenings and speaking first, because they acted against her gloomy forecast and gave her real results to judge instead of a fear.

qa.q: How does Raghav's experience of Ayesha change because of her new approach?
qa.a: Instead of a sigh, Raghav gets three clear fixes and a deadline she trusts him to meet, a demanding but reachable standard, and he meets it.

grounding: Shows, through a deskmate's account, a young architect who notices her gloomy forecast about reviews, acts against it by preparing and speaking first, treats the result as new evidence, and holds a junior to a high but fair standard.

passage: The week before Sinterklaas, Mr. Visser handed back the fractions test while everyone was still chattering about chocolate letters. Yuki saw 4 out of 10 in red and folded the paper into a tiny square. 'I am stupid,' she whispered to Jamal. 'I'm just bad at maths. I always will be.' Jamal had 5. He frowned at it, then shrugged. 'I didn't study the dividing part. I spent all Sunday on my Sinterklaas poem.' When Mr. Visser said anyone could take a retest on Friday, Jamal went up at break and asked for the practice sheet. Yuki stayed at her desk, pressing the folded square flat with her thumb. 'What's the point?' she said. Jamal came back and put a second practice sheet on her desk anyway.

qa.q: What mark did Yuki get on the fractions test?
qa.a: Yuki got 4 out of 10.

qa.q: What does Yuki folding the test into a tiny square suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: She seems ashamed and hopeless, as if the mark proves she is stupid for good, so she wants to hide it rather than fix it 😔

qa.q: What could help Yuki see the test the way Jamal does?
qa.a: Someone could ask her which part she got wrong and whether she studied it; tying the mark to one chapter makes it something she can change before Friday's retest.

qa.q: Why might Jamal react so differently to almost the same mark?
qa.a: Jamal explains it with a temporary reason, the dividing part he skipped, so trying again makes sense; Yuki explains it as permanent, so trying feels pointless.

grounding: Shows two children explaining the same setback as permanent or temporary, and how that decides whether they try again.

passage: Okay, Tejas, you asked why I didn't turn up for the second round of trials, so here it is. This Onam everyone's been at Ammachi's house, and I've been doing my usual thing: deciding I'm useless. I missed one header in the first round. One. And in my head it went: I'm slow, I'll always be slow, I'm slow at maths too, even my pookalam was the worst on the street this year. So why go back? I honestly thought I was just being realistic, you know? Then Ammachi found me sulking over my payasam and said, 'Jomon, you missed one ball, or you missed your whole life?' I laughed, but it stuck. With me it's never one bad thing. It's always everything, forever. Maybe that isn't the truth about me. Maybe it's just a habit I picked up somewhere, and habits can be unlearned.

qa.q: What happened to Jomon in the first round of the trials?
qa.a: Jomon missed one header.

qa.q: How did Jomon feel after missing the header, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Jomon felt defeated and useless: the one miss spread to maths and the pookalam too, and Jomon skipped the second round 😔

qa.q: What could Jomon ask the next time the 'I'm useless' story starts?
qa.a: Jomon could ask whether it was one miss or everything, whether it really lasts forever, and what one more try could change, just as Ammachi's question hinted.

qa.q: What might Ammachi have noticed while watching Jomon sulk over the payasam?
qa.a: Ammachi probably saw a grandchild blowing one missed ball up into a failed life, and her teasing question tried to shrink it back to its real size.

grounding: Shows a teenager who treats one setback as permanent and about everything, gives up quickly, and mistakes this habit for realism.

passage: The mid-semester results went up on the notice board outside the hostel mess at seven. Vandana found her roll number: organic chemistry, 11 out of 40. Back in the reading room she opened her notebook and wrote the sentence her head kept repeating: I am not made for science. Urmila, two desks away, watched her cross it out. Under it Vandana wrote: Evidence? Physics, 31. Lab reports, all signed. Then: Other reasons? Missed two mechanism lectures with fever. Revised by reading, never by drawing. 'You're not going to pretend you're fine?' Urmila asked. 'I'm not fine. I'm annoyed,' Vandana said. 'But it's one paper.' At the bottom she wrote a single line: Draw three mechanisms every night, from memory. Then she asked to borrow Urmila's notes from the two lectures she had missed.

qa.q: What mark did Vandana get in organic chemistry?
qa.a: Vandana got 11 out of 40.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling after seeing the result, and how does the passage show it?
qa.a: She was annoyed and shaken, saying 'I'm not fine', yet steady enough to test the harsh sentence against the facts instead of believing it.

qa.q: Which of Vandana's steps would help most before the next exam, and why?
qa.a: Drawing three mechanisms every night from memory, because it fixes the real gap, revising only by reading, rather than just trying to feel better.

qa.q: How might Urmila see the way Vandana handled the result?
qa.a: Urmila half expected false cheer, but sees Vandana admit being upset and still treat it as one paper, and can help directly by lending the missed lecture notes.

grounding: Shows a student who answers a harsh self-judgement after a failed exam by checking the evidence, weighing other explanations and choosing one change, without forced cheerfulness.

passage: Three days before the children's book fair, the forecast on my phone showed a grey cloud over Saturday. Our team lead Vasudha waved it away. 'Everything will be fine. It never rains in November.' Preeti, who sits across from me, didn't argue. She said, 'I think we'll get a good crowd. I also think we should be ready if it pours.' That afternoon I watched her phone the community hall down the road to hold it for Saturday, then order two rolls of plastic sheeting. Vasudha laughed and called her our weather minister. I laughed too, and felt bad about it later. On Saturday it rained at eleven. We moved forty boxes of books into the hall in twenty minutes, Preeti reading the list off her clipboard. Vasudha carried boxes without a word. I don't know what she was thinking. Relief, maybe, or embarrassment.

qa.q: What did Preeti arrange on the afternoon she heard the forecast?
qa.a: She phoned the community hall down the road to hold it for Saturday and ordered two rolls of plastic sheeting.

qa.q: How did the narrator feel, looking back, about laughing at Preeti's plan?
qa.a: The narrator felt bad about it, a little guilty, once the rain came and Preeti's preparation was what saved the fair.

qa.q: How is Preeti's hope different from Vasudha's in practice?
qa.a: Preeti expects a good crowd but still plans for rain with a backup hall and sheeting; Vasudha's cheer skips the forecast, so it protects nothing when the rain comes.

qa.q: What might Vasudha have felt while carrying the boxes in silence?
qa.a: Probably a mix of relief that the fair was saved and embarrassment that her 'everything will be fine' had ignored a real risk.

grounding: Shows an observer comparing a team lead's cheerful dismissal of a real risk with a colleague who hopes for the best and prepares for the worst.

passage:
Sunday. Farida sat on her friend Aparna's balcony, the prelims result open on her phone. She had missed the cut-off by six marks. 'Three years. I'm just not good enough.' Aparna didn't tell her it would be fine. She said, 'Six marks after three years. That's a lot to carry,' and let her cry.
Wednesday. Aparna brought a sheet of paper and drew two columns. Farida filled the first one fast: the result, the year gone. The second came slower: how she revised, the gaps in current affairs, the mock tests she kept skipping. 'Pick one,' Aparna said. Farida circled the mocks.
The next Saturday. At nine at night Farida messaged: 'Did a full mock. Terrible at current affairs. But now I know exactly where 🙂' Aparna sent back a thumbs-up and didn't add a speech.

qa.q: By how many marks did Farida miss the cut-off?
qa.a: Farida missed the cut-off by six marks.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling on Sunday, and what shows it?
qa.a: Farida felt hopeless and ashamed; she said 'I'm just not good enough' and cried after three years of work.

qa.q: What made Aparna's two-column sheet useful?
qa.a: It separated what could not change, the result and the lost year, from what could, and picking one item, the mock tests, turned despair into a step Farida could take 🙂

qa.q: What would change if Aparna had said 'It'll be fine' on Sunday?
qa.a: Farida might have felt brushed off and stopped talking; being heard first is what made her willing to sit down with the columns on Wednesday.

grounding: Shows a young adult who listens to a friend's despair without dismissing it, then helps separate what is fixed from what can change and find one small next step.

passage: At the nursery in Copenhagen, Freya's mum waved goodbye and Freya began to wail. Mina stopped stacking cups. Her chin wobbled. She looked at Freya, then at the door, and started crying too, though her own papa was still kneeling beside her. A boy by the window joined in. Mina's big brother Oskar, six, stared at them all. 'Nobody left you,' he said, puzzled, and held out her favourite red cup. Mina sniffed, took it, and leaned against his knee.

qa.q: What was Mina doing before Freya started to cry?
qa.a: Mina was stacking cups.

qa.q: Why did Mina start crying even though her papa was still there?
qa.a: Hearing Freya wail made Mina feel worried and sad too; she caught the upset without any reason of her own.

qa.q: How could a nursery teacher help when crying spreads like this?
qa.a: Comfort Freya calmly and quickly, and offer the others a familiar toy or a lap, the way Oskar offered the red cup.

qa.q: Why might Oskar be puzzled by Mina's tears?
qa.a: At six, Oskar looks for a reason, and nobody left Mina, so he doesn't see that her crying simply spread from Freya.

grounding: Shows one toddler's crying in a nursery spreading to others who become upset without knowing why.
